## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sakuṇajātaka* (also known as the *Javasakuṇajātaka*, Ja 308) is a canonical birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The Buddha delivered the tale while residing at Jetavana to address the ingratitude of Devadatta [SuttaCentral; Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1883].
Set in the past during the reign of King Brahmadatta in Benares, the story recounts a former life in which the Bodhisatta was born as a swift bird (woodpecker) [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The bird performed a benevolent service for a suffering lion by extracting a bone lodged in the beast's throat [Anandajoti 2010]. When the bird subsequently asks whether it might receive any favor or requital in return, the lion haughtily rebuffs the request, retorting that it was already a great mercy for a creature living between the jaws of a blood-drinking carnivore to have escaped with its life [Burlingame 1921; Anandajoti 2010]. In response, the bird reflects on the wisdom of quietly walking away from an ungrateful person without enmity or reproach (*akataññuṃ akattāraṃ*) [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the lion was Devadatta in an earlier existence, while the wise bird was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883].
Regarding parallels and text reuse, automated analysis by DharmaNexus detects three Pali-internal text-reuse matches totalling 724 characters between this text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Tatiyo bhāgo), with the primary overlap spanning segments §1.4–4.4 of this text and §197–205 of the commentary [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any verified cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Tibetan, or Chinese corpora [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
